card.name: Stave dancing
card.tagline: English country dancing carrying decorated friendly society poles over the shoulder.
card.profile: Stave dancing is a style of folk dance from the south-west of England, particularly Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire. Originating from nineteenth-century friendly society 'club walks', dancers perform set English country dance figures while carrying four- to six-foot wooden staves topped with brass or wooden emblems over their right shoulder. The movement blends double-stepping, a traveling polka or ranting step, and the Dorset skip-change step. Almost extinct by the late 1920s, the tradition was revived in the 1980s through the research and choreography of Roy Dommett.
card.insight: By 1928 stave dancing had nearly died out, but at 1930s club days in Henton, Somerset villagers packed marquees to watch Mendip elders carry brass-headed spears and step the board to accordion music.
card.profile_long:
Origins and History:
Stave dancing developed in the south-west of England, primarily in Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire, during the middle years of the nineteenth century. Its roots lie in the annual 'club walks' organised by local friendly societies. These societies provided sickness and death benefits to members and fostered fraternity through annual celebrations that included parades, church services, feasts, and music. Friendly society stewards and members carried decorated staves as symbols of office, mimicking civic dignitaries. During these processional perambulations and social stops, participants began performing country dances while holding their staves. Archival records note processional dancing with flower-topped poles in Shrawley, Worcestershire around 1880, and step dancing competitions at Henton club days. The tradition had largely faded by the late 1920s, with the last recorded classic instance at Shepton Beauchamp in 1928, though competitive step dancing with staves survived at Henton into the early 1930s.

How It Is Danced:
Stave dances adapt English country dance figures for dancers holding a stave over the right shoulder. Dancers perform in mixed groups arranged in sets of four, six, eight, or more. Key footwork includes double-stepping, a traveling 'ranting' or 'polka' step, and a 'chasing' step known as the Dorset skip-change step. While the staves remain anchored primarily on the shoulder during spatial movement, specific figures require dancers to raise staves high, twirl them overhead, or cross them to create arches and square 'rose' formations. Individual dances historically shared traits with broom dances. Known historical routines include versions of the Six Hand Reel, Four Hand Reels, Hunt the Squirrel, Up the Sides and Down the Middle, Haste to the Wedding, Pop Goes the Weasel, the Dorsetshire March, and Spithead Fleet.

Music and Instruments:
Stave dancing is accompanied by traditional English country dance tunes. Historical accounts document music provided by instruments such as the accordion, as played by J. Andrews of Godney for the Mendip step dancers at Henton. Tunes follow typical country dance meters and arrangements, providing clear rhythmic drive for traveling step-work and figure transitions.

Costume and Setting:
Historically, dancers wore their 'Sunday best' to satisfy friendly society mandates to be decently dressed. Stewards routinely wore black tailcoats, blue sashes, top hats adorned with blue ribbons or cockades, and white moleskin trousers. Friendly society staves were wooden poles four to six feet long, painted or striped, topped with wooden or brass emblems and adorned with blue ribbons or knots. Dancing took place outdoors during parish perambulations, at village stations, in churchyards, and inside festive marquees. Modern revival teams copy these Victorian dress standards, featuring top hats, sashes, and brass-tipped staves.

Occasions and Meaning:
Dancing occurred during annual friendly society club walks, held on holidays like Whit-Monday and Midsummer's Day, as well as village weddings. The staves symbolized civic duty, fraternity, and society leadership. Post-dinner step dancing competitions provided village entertainment and showcased physical agility among community members.

Notable Figures:
Roy Dommett was a former scientist and folk dance researcher who single-handedly driven the modern revival of stave dancing starting in the 1970s. After locating archival notes, manuscript details from Maud Karpeles, and society minute books, Dommett reconstructed and re-choreographed stave dances, teaching them to Morris teams like Bath City Morris and Abercorn Morris.

Regional Variants:
Different villages across Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire maintained unique dance lists and customs. Stourton Caundle preserved a distinct list of dance figures and choruses, while Fifehead Magdalen recorded specific country dance tunes. Buckhorn Weston was known for wedding stave reels, Henton was famous for Mendip step dancing competitions, and Shrawley in Worcestershire recorded processional pole dancing.

Lineage:
Stave dancing derives from Victorian friendly society civic processions and 19th-century English social country dancing. It forms a distinct regional branch of English folk dance alongside Morris and broom dancing, actively preserved today by teams like Somerset Morris, Fleur-de-Lys Morris, and Bradninch Millers.

sections.origins_and_history: Stave dancing originated in the south-west of England during the mid-nineteenth century, arising from friendly society 'club walks' in Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire. Friendly societies were fraternal organizations that provided sickness and death benefits while organising annual social parades, church services, and dinners. Members and stewards carried decorated ceremonial staves, which evolved into dance props as participants performed country dances and step dances along parish bounds and at village stops. Primary records include accounts of processional pole dancing in Shrawley around 1880 and competitive step dancing in Henton. The tradition mostly died out by the late 1920s, with a final recorded historic instance at Shepton Beauchamp in 1928, before being revived in the 1980s.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are performed in mixed sets of four, six, eight, or more dancers who carry a four- to six-foot stave over the right shoulder while executing English country dance figures. Basic steps include double-stepping, a traveling polka or 'ranting' step, and the Dorset skip-change step. While staves are primarily carried on the shoulder, specific figures involve forming elevated arches, twirling staves overhead, or raising staves in a overhead square formation known as a 'rose'. Historic routines include four-hand and six-hand reels, processional perambulations, and step-dancing displays.
sections.music_and_instruments: Stave dances are set to traditional English country dance tunes. Historic reports mention accordion music, such as performance by Mr. J. Andrews of Godney at Henton club days. Tunes listed in historical minute books include 'Haste to the Wedding', 'Pop Goes the Weasel', 'the Dorsetshire March', 'Spithead Fleet', and 'Hunt the Squirrel'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historical costume reflected friendly society rules requiring members to wear 'Sunday best'. Stewards typically wore black tailcoats, blue sashes, top hats decorated with blue ribbons or knots, and white moleskin trousers. Staves were wooden poles between four and six feet long, painted or striped like barber poles, topped with brass or wooden emblems and blue ribbons. Performance settings included outdoor parish perambulations, village halts, church walks, and marquee tents after annual dinners. Modern teams often reproduce these Victorian steward costumes.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Stave dancing took place during annual friendly society 'club walks' on Whit-Monday and Midsummer's Day, as well as community weddings. Staves carried symbolic weight as emblems of civic authority and fraternal unity. Competitive step dancing displays following annual dinners allowed local dancers to demonstrate agility and pride in their society's regional traditions.
sections.notable_figures: Roy Dommett, a scientist and folk dance researcher, recovered historical references and manuscripts (including notes collected by Maud Karpeles) in the 1970s and re-choreographed stave dances. He introduced these routines to sides such as Bath City Morris and Abercorn Morris, establishing the modern revival.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variations centered on specific villages in Dorset and Somerset. Stourton Caundle documented a distinct set of dance figures and choruses. Fifehead Magdalen kept minute books detailing specific dance titles practiced at walk stations. Buckhorn Weston was noted for wedding six-hand reels, while Henton featured competitive Mendip step dancing on wooden boards.
sections.lineage: Stave dancing bridges Victorian friendly society civic ritual and English social country dance. Related to broom dancing and Morris dance traditions, it went dormant in the 1930s until Roy Dommett's reconstruction revitalised it through modern teams including Somerset Morris, Fleur-de-Lys Morris, and Bradninch Millers.

basic_steps: Stave rest: Hold four-to-six foot pole securely resting over the right shoulder.
Dorset skip-change step: Step forward with rhythmic lift and skip action to travel within figures.
Ranting step: Execute a crisp traveling polka step maintaining set rhythm.
Double-stepping: Perform double-step footwork while navigating set formations.
Rose figure: Raise staves aloft together with four dancers to form a central square.
teaching.rhythm: Duple or triple meter traditional English country dance tunes.
teaching.formation: Mixed sets of four, six, eight, or more dancers.
teaching.level_notes: Requires coordination to balance a long stave over the shoulder while executing traveling country dance footwork.

claims.text: Stave dancing is a style of folk dance from the south-west of England, especially Somerset, Dorset, and Wiltshire.
Dancers carry long decorated poles known as staves over their shoulders during performance.
The tradition effectively died out in the 1920s before being revived in the 1980s.
Footwork includes double-stepping, ranting or polka steps, and the Dorset skip-change step.
Dancing staves evolved from ceremonial poles carried by friendly society stewards and members.
Competitive step dancing with staves survived into the early 1930s at Henton near Wells.
Roy Dommett re-discovered and regenerated interest in stave dancing starting in the 1970s.

gaps: No commercial recordings or albums specifically documenting original stave dance music were listed in sources.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Lively duple or triple country dance pulse supporting polka and skip-change traveling steps
music_profile.musical_form: AABB binary country dance tune structure
music_profile.sound_description: Lively traditional English country dance melodies driven by accordion accompaniment, characterized by clear rhythmic cadence suitable for stepping and processional figures.

movement_profile.posture: Upright body posture, holding a long wooden stave resting over the right shoulder.
movement_profile.footwork: Double-stepping, ranting/polka traveling step, Dorset skip-change step, and board step dancing.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Right arm securing the stave over the right shoulder; staves are raised aloft to form arches or overhead square rose figures, or twirled overhead.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Engaged and steady torso to maintain pole balance while executing footwork.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Processional paths or sets of four, six, eight, or more dancers executing country dance figures.
movement_profile.partnering: Set formation partnering; interaction via stave arches and shared rose figures.

signature_moves.name: Rose figure
signature_moves.description: Four dancers raise their staves aloft together to form a square canopy.

signature_moves.name: Stave arch
signature_moves.description: Dancers raise staves overhead to create archways for partners to pass under.

signature_moves.name: Overhead twirl
signature_moves.description: Individual dancer twirls the stave overhead as part of a solo step segment.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Ground-based stepping with light skipping hops in Dorset skip-change steps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Dropping or swinging staves unsafely in tight set formations.

episode_brief.title_hook: Poles, Polkas, and Parades: The Stave Dancers of Somerset
episode_brief.logline: Discover how 19th-century friendly society stewards turned ceremonial poles into a vibrant English folk dance tradition.
beats: Open on a parade of dancers wearing top hats and holding brass-topped staves over their shoulders.
Explore the 19th-century friendly society roots and annual Whit-Monday club walks in Dorset and Somerset.
Demonstrate the essential Dorset skip-change and ranting steps across wooden floorboards.
Detail Roy Dommett's 1970s archival breakthrough and dance reconstruction.
Perform a full set featuring the four-dancer rose figure with overhead staves.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master stave carriage and basic traveling step.
drills: Practice posture while balancing pole over right shoulder.
Perform Dorset skip-change step along a straight line.
Perform ranting polka step in sets of four.
Form arches using staves while maintaining step rhythm.
Perform individual overhead stave twirl combined with step dancing.
